A whack is a sharp, hard hit — the kind that makes a loud smacking sound.

She gave the stuck drawer a good whack, and it finally opened.
The ball flew across the field after one clean whack.

Think of a cricket bat hitting a ball, a hammer striking a nail, or a hand slapping a table in frustration. That sudden, forceful contact — and the sound it produces — is a whack. The word itself almost sounds like the action.

"Whack" also means someone's fair share of something, especially money or resources. This is common in informal British English.

Everyone did equal work, so everyone should get an equal whack of the profits.
He paid his whack toward the rent and expected the others to do the same.

Here, "whack" functions just like "portion" or "cut." You can think of it as the slice of a pie that belongs to you.

You'll often see "whack" used to mean a go at something — a try or attempt.

I've never played chess before, but I'll have a whack at it.
Give it a whack — you might surprise yourself.

The phrase here is almost always "have a whack at" something. It's light and casual in tone, suggesting you're not under pressure — just giving something a shot.

In informal British English, "whack" can also describe a large quantity or the highest possible level of something — especially in the phrases top whack and full whack.

The hotel charges top whack during the holiday season. (= the highest possible price)
He was paying full whack for a service he barely used. (= the full, undisc­ounted price)
A whack of tourists descended on the small village. (= a large number)

Here, the word signals scale — something is at its maximum, or there's simply a lot of it.
The essential phrase: out of whack

This is probably the single most important phrase built from the noun "whack," and you will encounter it constantly.

Out of whack means: not working correctly; misaligned; in a disordered or irregular state.

It describes anything — a machine, a system, a relationship, a body — that has lost its proper balance or functioning.

My sleep schedule is completely out of whack since I changed time zones.
The engine sounds wrong — something must be out of whack.
Ever since they had that argument, the whole team dynamic has been out of whack.

Notice that it doesn't have to refer to a physical object. You can use it for anything that feels off — finances, plans, emotions, timing. The opposite idea would be: everything is in order, working smoothly, as it should be.

MeaningIn a sentence

Here's a quick mental map instead:

  • A hit → One whack of the hammer did the job.
  • A share → Everyone gets their fair whack.
  • An attempt → Have a whack at it.
  • A large amount / max price → They charged top whack.
  • Out of order → Something's out of whack.

The thread connecting most of these is force or impact — either a literal strike, or the idea of something hitting a limit (top whack), or something that has been knocked out of its proper state (out of whack).

"Whack" as a noun is informal. You'd use it in casual speech, friendly writing, or relaxed conversation — not in formal essays or professional reports. It carries an energetic, slightly punchy quality, which makes sense given its literal meaning. It's widely used in both British and American English, though the "share" and "top whack" meanings are more distinctly British.
